paragraphs: Swamiji said the Buddha's last words always sent a thrill through his heart, and he loved to tell how the great teacher passed away.

Buddha was old, ill and close to death when an invitation came from Chanda, an outcaste scorned by society, who lived on the flesh of dead animals and was not even allowed into the cities. Buddha went with his disciples. Poor Chanda, wanting to honour his guest with the best he knew, served him a large meal of rice and pork.

The disciples hesitated and the Master told them not to eat, as it would harm them. But he himself sat down quietly and ate what Chanda had prepared. The teacher of equality would not refuse the outcaste's food.

Death was already approaching. Buddha asked for something to be spread under a tree, and lay down there, no longer able to sit up. His first thought was for his host: go and tell Chanda, he said, that he has been one of my greatest benefactors, for through his meal I am entering Nirvana.

People kept arriving to be taught. The disciples tried to keep them away, but each time Buddha asked that they be let in. To Ananda and the others he said: do not weep or think of me; work out your own salvation with diligence. Each of you is just what I am; what I am, I made myself, so struggle and become what I am.

His final teaching was perhaps the most memorable of all: don't believe something just because an old book says it, or your father believed it, or others do. Test everything and try it yourself; and if you find it good for many, share it with all. With these words, the Master passed away.
learn: Buddha's last day shows respect for every person, regardless of status, and gratitude even toward someone whose gift harmed him. His parting advice is a great rule for any age of information overload: test ideas yourself, and share what genuinely helps others.
